paras: The attempted lynching of Edward Johnson took place in Emporia, Kansas, on the evening of August 5, 1881, when a crowd of a hundred to three hundred men gathered at the Lyon county jail to hang Johnson, a Black man accused of killing Deputy Sheriff James Spillman. Johnson escaped harm because Sheriff Moon had already sent him under guard to Cottonwood Falls, and he was later committed to the asylum at Ossawatomie. The Emporia Weekly News condemned the gathering as mob law that would have disgraced the town and praised the sheriff for averting it.

Johnson, described by the News as 'a light colored negro' of about forty-five and a one-legged Civil War pensioner from Indiana, had been held in the county jail since early May, when he was accused of a 'deadly assault' on Marshal Johnson and B. F. Romaine during his arrest for carrying concealed weapons. A jury had adjudged him insane on July 12.

On the evening of Thursday, August 4, Spillman drove Johnson to Elbert Love's house in Stringtown to collect a trunk, and there, according to the News, Johnson stabbed him with a butcher knife; Spillman died soon after. A coroner's jury sat until four in the morning and found the killing felonious. A crowd at the court house gate that night showed 'fierce indignation' without violence, and the paper reported that many Black residents who knew Johnson insisted he was sane and called for him to be 'summarily hung'.

Warned during the day of a plan to lynch Johnson, Sheriff Moon sent him toward Cottonwood Falls at about dusk in L. F. Pruyne's spring wagon, guarded by Marshal Johnson, Lee Vernon and B. F. Romaine. At about nine o'clock a crowd, including a delegation of miners from Osage City who had ridden in that afternoon and whom the News called 'the leading spirits of the uprising', gathered at the jail windows in the court house yard, some holding ropes. Moon addressed the crowd and said Johnson had been gone for hours; many accepted his word, but others demanded a search, and a committee went through the cells and confirmed it.

By then the crowd had grown to 'two or three hundred' and filled the south part of the yard. Word spread that the prisoner was on the road to Cottonwood Falls, and a party of horsemen was reported to have set off, but the surviving text of the report breaks off at that point. The wagon reached Cottonwood Falls at one o'clock Saturday morning, where Johnson, who the News said showed 'abject terror' on the road, was handed to the sheriff there.

The News denied rumors that Johnson had been lynched at Cottonwood Falls on Saturday night. On Monday night he passed through Emporia by train, guarded by a Cottonwood Falls officer and Moon, on his way to the Ossawatomie asylum. No report of arrests of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

Feeling ran beyond Emporia: a country correspondent wrote on August 6 that crowds there were being organized to go to the town and 'lynch the perpetrator of the crime'. Spillman was buried after a funeral in the court house yard on Sunday, which the paper called the largest ever held in Emporia.

All known coverage comes from the August 11 issue of the Emporia Weekly News, which collected the week's daily reports; no other paper's account has been found. Its editorial 'Not to be Countenanced' called the gathering a 'reprehensible undertaking' and warned that mob law led to 'anarchy and social chaos', resting much of its case on the town's reputation 'at home and abroad'. A second piece, 'Deserves Commendation', praised Moon and called the demonstration 'a farce rather than a tragedy', while the news report ran under the headline 'A Close Call for Johnson'.
The same paper consistently called Johnson 'the murderer' and 'the insane negro', and argued that he should never again be allowed to go free.

The main report dates the gathering to 'Thursday evening', the night of the killing, but the wagon's arrival at Cottonwood Falls at 1 a.m. Saturday after a five-hour drive places it on Friday, August 5.

bases: A crowd with ropes assembled at the Lyon county jail to take Edward Johnson out and hang him for killing Deputy Sheriff Spillman, and was foiled only because the sheriff had already removed him (A1, A6, A7).

A crowd of a hundred to three hundred men gathered to hang Johnson for the killing of a deputy sheriff, an extralegal act under a pretext of justice (A1, A6), but Johnson had been taken to Cottonwood Falls and was not harmed (A7, A8); this was an attempted lynching.
Every report comes from one issue of one paper, the Emporia Weekly News of August 11, 1881, though its several items agree on the core event (A1, A6, A7).

accounts.label: Emporia News report
accounts.gist: A crowd led by Osage City miners, some with ropes, gathered at the jail about 9 pm to lynch Johnson; Sheriff Moon told them he was gone, a committee confirmed it, and the crowd of two or three hundred learned he was on the road to Cottonwood Falls.

accounts.label: Sheriff Moon's arrangements, as told by the News
accounts.gist: Warned during the day, Moon had Johnson driven out at dusk under guard; he reached Cottonwood Falls at 1 a.m. Saturday, voicing regret for the killing and terror on the road.

accounts.label: News editorial
accounts.gist: The gathering of a hundred or more men was a lawless project that would have disgraced Emporia, averted by Moon's foresight.

framing.detail: Editorial 'NOT TO BE COUNTENANCED' called the gathering a 'reprehensible undertaking' and mob law leading to 'anarchy', mainly as a danger to Emporia's reputation, while calling Johnson 'his murderer' and 'the insane negro'.
Headline 'A CLOSE CALL FOR JOHNSON' and the follow-up 'DESERVES COMMENDATION' credited Sheriff Moon and dismissed the demonstration as 'a farce rather than a tragedy'.

The evening before Johnson reached Cottonwood Falls at 1 a.m. Saturday, i.e., Friday, August 5

conflicts.note: The killing took place Thursday about 8:30 pm and the inquest ran until 4 a.m.; the plan was 'arranged during the day' and the miners came 'in the afternoon', so 'Thursday' in A6 cannot be the day of the killing; Friday, August 5, fits A7's timeline and the editorial's 'last evening' after 'the mournful tragedy of Thursday night' (A1, A9).
Not strictly in conflict: the report says the crowd grew to two or three hundred by the end of the jail search.
